notes.meaning: David cries out for God's free mercy while trapped in the city of Gath among dangerous enemies. Cruel men hound him without stopping, eager to crush and swallow him up like wild beasts. When we find no mercy or safety among people, we can always run to God for help.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The tune title may refer to a musical style, the name of a well-known melody, or a specific instrument.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that Gath represents strangers who refuse Christ, and that the believer must face both visible human foes and the invisible devil.

notes.meaning: David's foes watch him closely and hunt him all day long. They attack him in large numbers with great pride from their high positions of power. Yet David looks above their authority to the God who rules over all.

David admits that he feels real fear when facing deadly peril. Instead of being paralyzed, he deliberately places his confidence in the Lord. Faith and fear can happen at the same time, but true faith turns our fears toward God.

David praises God for His promises even before those promises are completely fulfilled. Because he relies on the almighty Creator, he does not dread mortal humans who are only frail flesh. Trusting God's sure word removes the crippling fear of what people might do to us.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: An early Greek translation reads 'my words' instead of 'his word,' leading some scholars to read the line as David praising God with his own speech.

notes.meaning: David's enemies twist his words out of shape to make him look guilty, thinking only of how to ruin him. They gather in secret, lay hidden traps, and follow his footsteps like hunters tracking their prey to take his life. God sees the unfair schemes of those who try to harm His servants.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine saw these lurking plotters as a picture of false brothers inside the church who betray believers, just as Judas betrayed Christ.

notes.meaning: David asks whether wicked men can really escape punishment through their evil tricks. He knows that wickedness gives no real safety before a holy God, so he asks the Lord in righteous anger to bring down these violent foes.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine read the Latin text as 'For nothing You shall save them,' understanding it as salvation by God's free grace without any human merit, and urged Christians to pray for their enemies.

notes.meaning: David finds deep comfort in knowing that God counts every step of his wandering as a fugitive. He asks God to collect his tears as if in a leather bottle and record them in His book of remembrance. God tenderly values our sorrows and never forgets a single tear His people cry.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest 'wanderings' describes inward tossing and mental restlessness rather than physical journeys.

notes.meaning: David is sure that his enemies will be forced to turn back the moment he cries out in prayer. He knows with complete confidence that God is on his side to defend him. Sincere prayer is a powerful weapon that brings the Lord's help into our battles.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine suggested that the turning back of enemies can work for their own good by leading them to turn away from sin.

notes.meaning: David repeats his joyful chorus, praising God's word and using His personal name, the Lord. Because his trust is firmly fixed on God, his fear of people disappears. Believers can stand strong against threats because mere humans cannot overturn God's good plans for them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the second line mentioning the LORD as a later addition that interrupts the regular chorus.

notes.meaning: David remembers the vows—sacred promises made to God—that he made when he was in deep trouble. Now that he looks ahead to safety, he gladly resolves to offer sacrifices and songs of thanksgiving. When God brings us through hard times, we should always keep our promises to thank Him.

God rescued David's life from death and kept his feet from stumbling into disaster or sin. David's greatest goal in being delivered is to walk in God's favor and serve Him faithfully during his life on earth. When the Lord preserves our lives, He frees us to live in His joyful presence.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some translations read the middle part as a question, asking if God has not already kept his feet from falling to complete His past rescue.
